easy.heading: Warming Up With Today's Easy Grid
easy.body:
Starting my morning with the easy puzzle was exactly what I needed to get my brain in gear. I immediately looked at the bottom right corner where there was a sum region asking for a total of 10 in cells (2,1) and (2,2). Since the dominoes available were [5,2], [6,6], [3,4], and [0,4], I knew that the [6,6] tile had to be involved somehow because 10 is such a high number for this grid. I placed the [6,6] tile vertically at (1,2) and (2,2), which gave me a 6 at cell (2,2). To finish off that sum of 10, I needed a 4 at cell (2,1).

That 4 at (2,1) was part of the domino at (2,0) and (2,1), so I used the [0,4] tile there. This meant cell (2,0) was a 0. Looking at the next sum region for cells (1,0) and (2,0) which needed to total 4, I realized (1,0) had to be a 4. I used the [3,4] domino for the left side at (0,0) and (1,0). Finally, I tucked the [5,2] domino into the remaining spots at (0,1) and (0,2). It all clicked into place when I checked the less than 10 constraint at (0,2) and (1,2), which ended up being 2 plus 6, totaling 8. A perfect fit!
easy.tips: Try looking for the biggest sum constraints first because they usually limit your domino choices the most. Also, always double check your empty cells to make sure you didn't accidentally try to place a pip where it doesn't belong.

medium.heading: Zeros Are My New Best Friends
medium.body:
The medium puzzle felt like a nice step up, mainly because of those less than 1 constraints at (1,3) and (3,4). Since the only number less than 1 in this game is zero, those spots were essentially freebies! I knew (1,3) and (3,4) had to be zeros. This helped me narrow down my dominoes, as I had [2,0], [0,6], and [1,0] to work with. I placed the [2,0] domino at (3,3) and (3,4), which put a 2 at (3,3). This was great because (3,2) and (3,3) were in an equals region, meaning (3,2) had to be a 2 as well.

From there, the middle of the board started to fill in. I had a sum of 4 to hit at (3,0) and (3,1), and another sum of 4 at (1,1) and (1,0). By carefully checking which dominoes had the right values, I placed the [3,2] tile across (3,1) and (3,2), which satisfied the equals region. The puzzle really rewarded looking at how the regions overlapped. Once I got the zeros placed, the rest of the numbers just seemed to flow naturally into their spots. Ian Livengood really knows how to make these grids feel like a satisfying logic loop.
medium.tips: When you see a less than 1 constraint, immediately mark it as a zero to clear up your options. Always look for equals regions that connect two different dominoes, as they act like a bridge for your logic.

hard.heading: Taming The Equalizer Challenge
hard.body:
Rodolfo Kurchan really outdid himself with this hard grid! The standout feature was that massive five-cell equals region covering (0,2), (1,2), (1,3), (1,4), and (2,2). I spent a good few minutes just staring at the domino list to see which number appeared often enough to fill those spots. I also noticed the sum 2 constraint for cell (0,5), which meant that cell had to be a 2. Using the [1,2] domino at (0,4) and (0,5) gave me a 1 at (0,4). This helped me solve the sum 2 region at (0,3) and (0,4) because (0,3) then had to be a 1.

The real breakthrough came when I realized the number 3 was the key for the large equals regions. By placing 3s in the cells like (1,3) and (1,2), everything else started to cascade. I used the [1,3] domino at (0,3) and (1,3), which confirmed that the big equals region was all 3s. This meant I could place [3,3] at (0,2) and (1,2). The bottom right area with the unequal constraint was the last hurdle, but by then, I only had a few tiles left, like [5,5] and [3,6], which made the final placements much more manageable. It was a tough nut to crack, but so rewarding once those 3s lined up!
hard.tips: In large puzzles, count how many times each pip value appears in your domino list to see which numbers can fit into large equals regions. Don't be afraid to work from the corners inward, as single-cell sum regions are basically free clues.

explanation.learned: Today I really learned the power of the equals constraint. In the hard puzzle, seeing that five different cells had to share the same value completely changed how I looked at my domino list. It turns the game into a bit of a scavenger hunt for a specific digit. I also realized that even in a complex grid, those tiny sum 2 or sum 1 regions are your best friend for getting a foot in the door.

faqs.question: What does the less than constraint mean in NYT Pips?
faqs.answer: It means the sum of the pips in that specific region must be less than the number shown. If it is a single cell and says less than 1, that cell must contain a zero.

faqs.question: How do you handle empty cells in a Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: Empty cells are spots where no domino pips are placed. They usually act as spacers or are part of regions where their value is effectively zero for sum calculations.

faqs.question: Are dominoes used more than once in Pips?
faqs.answer: No, each domino from the provided list is used exactly once. This is a key part of the strategy because once you place a tile, it is off the board for the rest of your logic.

faqs.question: What is the best way to start a hard NYT Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: Look for the most restrictive regions first. This includes regions with very small sums, very large sums, or equals regions that cover many cells. These often have only one or two possible solutions.

faqs.question: Can dominoes be placed diagonally?
faqs.answer: No, dominoes must always be placed either horizontally or vertically, covering two adjacent cells in the grid.
